blocks.text: Quillon Harbor Advisors LLC

Quillon Harbor Advisors is a mergers and acquisitions advisory for the lower middle market, and the greater part of our work is helping the founder of an industrial or business-services company sell the business on terms that reflect what it took to build it. Alongside that sell-side practice we run acquisition searches for private-equity sponsors assembling a platform in a sector we know, and now and then we give a board an independent opinion on the fairness of a transaction it has been asked to approve. Whichever of these brings a client to us, the people who meet that client at the outset are the people who do the work, and a partner stays with the mandate until it is finished.
What we do, and the companies we do it for

rows: Sell-side advisory

Preparing the business and its owner for a sale, writing the materials a buyer will read, building and contacting a researched list of acquirers, managing confidentiality agreements and diligence, and negotiating through to a signed purchase agreement
Founder-owned companies in industrial manufacturing and distribution, and in business services
Buy-side search programs

Agreeing a candidate universe with the sponsor, screening it against the sponsor's criteria, approaching the companies that survive the screen, executing NDAs with those willing to talk, and carrying the most promising conversations through to offers
Private-equity sponsors building a platform by acquisition in an industrial or business-services sector
Fairness opinions
An independent assessment, for the directors, of whether the consideration in a proposed transaction is fair from a financial point of view, supported by the valuation work behind it
Boards and board committees of companies in the same sectors, where the directors want a view from an adviser with no stake in the outcome

blocks.text: The three lines have more in common than a table can show. The discipline that narrows a sponsor's universe to a handful of real candidates is the same one that produces a buyer list a seller can trust, and the valuation work underneath every sale process is what allows us to give a board an opinion we are prepared to stand behind.

We keep our deal teams small on purpose, so that an owner hears the same three or four names from the first meeting onward, and so that the analyst building a buyer list or a target screen sits close enough to the partner to be asked why a company is on it. Every count that appears in a document we send, whether of buyers contacted, agreements executed or offers received, is one we can reconcile to the record underneath it. When a figure changes, as figures do in the middle of a process, it changes everywhere at once, and the client hears about it from us before reading it anywhere else.
Clients we have advised

What follows is a sample of our client work and not an account of all of it, offered because a firm is most fairly judged by the companies that have trusted it with a decision of this weight. In recent years we have acted for {{fact:f:E-2014-001.client}}, for {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}}, and for {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}, and in each of those engagements a small and settled team carried the work, with a partner reading every document before it went out. We are grateful to each of them, and we keep the details of what we did for them, as we keep every client's, inside the firm.

Amanda Thomas, our Compliance Manager, is responsible for that discipline across the firm: she runs our conflict checks and confidentiality logs, reviews the wording of anything that touches a regulated question, and confirms, before a document circulates, that a company we are marketing is described in it only by its sector and its revenue band. Her reminders to the deal teams tend to arrive with a short explanation of why each rule exists, and the teams are better for it.

Every engagement letter and fairness opinion that leaves the firm has been read first by Heather Delacruz, our Managing Partner, and she also takes the first meeting with any owner, sponsor or board considering work with us. That meeting is the place to begin, and she will use it to explain how a process with us would unfold, stage by stage, before anything is signed.

James Lawson has joined the advisory practice as an Analyst, and with this note the firm welcomes him and sets down the arrangements for his first week, so that none of them rest on anyone's memory. He reports to Mark Allen, Partner, and will start on our sell-side mandates, drafting the teasers and process letters that carry a confidential sale from its first contact with buyers onward. He has already shown an instinct for the firm's confidentiality conventions that most new analysts take months to absorb, describing a target by its sector and revenue band without needing the reminder.

blocks.text: For anything on a live mandate James should go first to Mark Allen, and he should feel free to bring a half-finished draft instead of polishing it alone. A question about whether a target may be named in a given document, or about who may be let into a data room, belongs with compliance before the document goes anywhere, and the operations team handles equipment, access and expenses. Process letters carry the firm's name to every buyer, so they go to Heather Delacruz before they leave the building, and she reads them for any word that promises more than the process can deliver; James should not be discouraged if what she strikes first is one of his caveats.

His first piece of work is a draft teaser for a current sell-side mandate, which Mark Allen will go through with him line by line as soon as the first version is done, and the reconciliation of that mandate's buyer counts will follow once the teaser is settled.

We are glad to welcome Michael Duffy to the advisory practice as an Analyst. He reports to Mark Allen, Partner, and his early work will sit close to the sellers we represent, in the working sessions with a company's controller where the numbers behind a sale are gathered, questioned and set down in a form a buyer's diligence team can test. Michael has already shown a care with file names and draft labels that the rest of us may come to envy, and on a deal team where three people can be editing the same schedule in a single week it is a habit we intend to protect.

blocks.text: His first review will come toward the end of the summer. Mark Allen will lead it, with Heather Delacruz joining for the second half of the conversation, and it will be built around two pieces of Michael's own work, a note from a controller session and a section of a marketing document, each read beside the material it drew on. The question throughout will be whether a reader who was not in the room would reach the point without help, and Michael's own short account of his first months, written beforehand, goes in his file with Mark's notes of the meeting.

His first controller session is on a current sell-side mandate, and Mark Allen will brief him on the company and its open questions before he goes in. Michael should bring the note of that session to Mark the same afternoon, while the conversation is still fresh enough to settle any point the note leaves uncertain.

John Bauer has come to us as an Analyst at a time when bringing someone new into a firm takes more deliberate effort than usual, since most of us are still working from home and a deal team's day runs largely through video calls and the shared drive. The partners are grateful for the patience he has shown with that arrangement, and the deal team now begins each morning with a short call so that he is never left guessing what it needs from him. Heather Delacruz will meet him, by video for now, before his first month is out, to talk about the firm and about the owners we advise.

John reports to Mark Allen, Partner, and sits in the advisory practice with the analysts who build the screens, buyer lists and comparable-transaction tables that our partners take into a meeting with an owner or a sponsor. Most of his early work will be on buy-side search programs, where a sponsor's universe of candidates narrows week by week and nearly every document we send states some count of how far it has come. Those counts must agree with one another from the first memo to the last, and an analyst who holds a table back until it is complete is exactly the person we want keeping them.

In his first months we will ask John for reproducibility above all, so that every count he reports can be rebuilt from the screening log and every table carries its source and the date of the data it draws on. Where something is uncertain, the uncertainty belongs in the cover note, stated once and plainly, and not spread across the figures, so that a partner reading his table can quote it without first asking which of the numbers are firm. We will also ask him to write to owners in the register the partners use, which is warmer and plainer than most new analysts expect, and Mark Allen will read his first client-facing drafts with that in mind.

The first task on his desk is reconciling the candidate counts across every document issued so far on a current buy-side program, from the opening screen to the most recent update to the sponsor, and Mark Allen will go over the reconciliation with him on a call once the first pass is done.
About Quillon Harbor Advisors

Most of the companies we advise have belonged to one founder or one family for most of their history, and the decision to sell such a company, or to build a platform by buying several like it, is one its owner or sponsor usually makes only once. Quillon Harbor Advisors is a lower-middle-market mergers and acquisitions advisory that exists to give those decisions the advice they deserve, working with the owners of industrial and business-services companies, with the private-equity sponsors consolidating those sectors, and with the boards that need an independent read on a transaction. We keep our teams small and our partners close to the work, and we write everything we produce with the expectation that a board will read it and that a lawyer may later quote it.
How the practice is organized

items: Sell-side advisory. We prepare a founder-owned business and its owner for a sale, build and contact a researched list of buyers, run a confidential marketing process, and negotiate on the owner's behalf through signing and closing. The owner hears from a partner at every stage, and the analysis beneath each conversation is built to survive a buyer's diligence.

Buy-side search programs. For a private-equity platform consolidating a sector, we define a universe of candidate companies, screen it against the sponsor's criteria, approach the companies that survive the screen, execute NDAs with those willing to talk, and carry the strongest conversations to an offer.

Fairness opinions. For a board or a committee of its directors, we give an independent view of whether the consideration in a proposed transaction is fair from a financial point of view, supported by our own valuation work and set out in a letter the directors can rely on. We accept that work only where we have no stake in the outcome.

blocks.text: Whichever line a client engages, the work leaves a record behind it. A sponsor can see how many candidates entered the screen and how many survived each stage, and a seller can see every buyer approached, every NDA signed and every indication received, with each count reconciled from one document to the next.

For an owner, a sale is rarely only a financial event, and we explain each stage of a process before it begins, from the first conversations with buyers to the confirmatory diligence that follows a letter of intent, so that nothing in the sequence arrives as a surprise. We also say plainly when a stage is likely to take longer than anyone would like. This year a good many of those explanations have been given by video instead of across a table, and the sequence itself has not changed.

Confidentiality is part of how we write. In anything that circulates, a company we are marketing is described by its sector and its revenue band, and its name appears only in documents that are already privileged, a habit our clients tend to notice in the first week of an engagement.
Some of the clients we have served

We are glad to be able to name some of the clients we have advised, and we offer them as examples of the practice, not as a list of everyone it has served. Our engagements for {{fact:f:E-2014-001.client}}, for {{fact:f:E-2015-001.client}} and for {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}} belong to the firm's earlier years, and our more recent work has included engagements for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} and for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}. In each of them the same small team carried the engagement from the first meeting onward, every number we put in front of the client could be traced to its source, and the particulars of the work remain the client's own.

Inquiries about any of this work come to Heather Delacruz, our Managing Partner, who reads every engagement letter and fairness opinion before it leaves the firm. The next step for an owner, a sponsor or a board weighing a transaction is a first conversation with her about the business and about what its owners hope the transaction will accomplish, after which she will set out in writing how we would propose to run the work and who from the firm would run it.

With Kimberly Harris, who joins the advisory practice as an Analyst, the research behind our first meetings with founders gains someone with a real ear for what an owner says and what he or she means by it. She reports to Mark Allen, Partner, and her early work will be the company profiles and ownership backgrounds that a partner reads before sitting down with a founder for the first time. What follows records the arrangements for her first week and the people she should look to for help.

blocks.text: Mark Allen is her first call on anything to do with a live mandate, from which companies belong in a batch of profiles to how much background a partner wants before meeting a founder, and when two of her sources disagree about who owns a company or how long they have owned it, he would like to see both before she chooses between them. Questions about what may be named, in which document and for whose eyes, go to compliance, while the operations team looks after equipment, systems and the practical business of the office. Heather Delacruz is glad to be asked about the register in which we write to owners, which a new analyst usually finds is the hardest thing here to learn from a template.
Her first assignment is a set of ownership profiles for the candidates still in that program's screen, and Mark Allen will read the first two with her before she starts on the rest.
